newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate panel moves climate change resolution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate panel moves climate change resolution.

text.p: A U.S. Senate panel on Thursday approved a resolution calling for developing countries to help fight global warming, but a Democrat said he wanted changes to keep the resolution from blocking an international climate change treaty.
"A lot of people are describing this particular resolution as a treaty-killer," Massachusetts Democrat John Kerry told the Foreign Operations Committee.

But the panel passed the measure quickly on a voice vote, saying there would be later talks to make changes in the resolution pushed by West Virginia Democrat Robert Byrd and Nebraska Republican Chuck Hagel.

While the resolution is a non-binding "sense of the Senate," to date it has signatures of 65 senators and is viewed as a barometer of support for the administration's efforts to get a global warming treaty, which would be subject to Senate approval.

The resolution calls for developing countries to commit to limiting their heat-trapping pollution from burning fossil fuels in the same time frame that industrialised countries agree to in negotiations that are to end in December.

Kerry called this "a 180 degree reversal of the Berlin mandate" in which industrialised countries agreed they should make binding commitments to reduce their pollution, but not developing countries which so far have contributed little to the carbon gas build-up problem.
Kerry said he expected a number of senators did not know potential effects of the resolution they signed, and said the language needed to be clarified.
"We would have effectively created a dynamic that allows people to walk away from the treaty," Kerry said.

"There's no way developing nations ought to be expected to ante up within six months, within the very same compliance period, the exact same reduction levels as the industrialised countries that are the problem," he said.
A spokeswoman for Byrd said the intent of the resolution was that all countries should have commitments, but the degree and start-up times would vary among developing countries.

Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth, appearing at a Senate Environment Committee hearing on Thursday, said the Clinton administration agreed with the thrust of the Byrd-Hagel resolution, and said it did not specify the pollution curbs or obligations developing countries should have.

The administration has called for developing countries to agree to future negotiations for binding commitments to curb pollution from burning fossil fuels. In the meantime, it says they should take steps such as reducing energy subsidies and improving conservation to cut pollution.
